items.title: Five Kinds of Stinginess That Cost a Practitioner Both Merit and Liberation, and the Five Hindrances That Ruin Precepts, Learning, and Meditation in Sequence

items.zh: 又有五種失利養因行，亦是背涅槃因行。謂若於是處受用利養，若從彼得，若所得物，若所為得，若如是得，於此諸處心生吝惜。又有五法，令修行者先毀淨戒、多聞，後虧止觀善軛。謂於諸欲中心生愛染，於能覺發憶念教授教誡者所心生瞋恚，未受尸羅令其不受；雖先受得後令棄捨，或使穿穴。耽著惛睡，恒不寂靜，染污追悔，常懷疑惑，於所聞法不能領受；雖初領受，尋即忘失；雖不忘失，不證決定。
items.en: There are also five causes leading to the loss of one's own gains, which are likewise causes turning one away from nirvāṇa: begrudging the place where offerings are received, the patron from whom they come, the object received, the praise thereby gained, or the teaching thereby attained — feeling stingy in any of these five respects. There are also five things that first cause a practitioner to violate pure precepts and learning, and thereafter impair the good yoke of calm and insight: giving rise to defiled craving towards sensory desires; giving rise to hatred towards those who awaken correct mindfulness through instruction and admonition — preventing one not yet ordained from being ordained, and causing one already ordained to abandon or breach the precepts; indulging in torpor and drowsiness; being constantly unsettled; harbouring defiled regret; and constantly holding doubt — such that the teaching once heard cannot be absorbed, or, if absorbed, is soon forgotten, or, if not forgotten, never yields settled certainty.

items.title: The Five Lower Fetters and Five Upper Fetters, Named and Explained in Full

items.zh: 又有二種下分。謂見道是修道下分，欲界是色、無色界下分。約此二種下分，說五下分結。依初下分，說薩迦耶見、戒禁取、疑；依第二下分，說貪欲、瞋恚。又有二種上分。謂色界及無色界。依此二種上分，說五上分結。或有無差別結。謂色貪、無色貪。或有有差別結。謂愛上靜慮者掉，慢上靜慮者慢，無明上靜慮者無明。
items.en: There are also two lower divisions: the path of seeing is the lower division of the path of cultivation, and the desire realm is the lower division relative to the form and formless realms. In dependence on these two lower divisions, the five lower fetters are spoken of: in dependence on the first, self-view, attachment to wrong rules and rites, and doubt; in dependence on the second, craving and hostility. There are also two upper divisions: the form realm and the formless realm. In dependence on these two upper divisions, the five upper fetters are spoken of. Some are undifferentiated fetters: craving for the form realm and craving for the formless realm. Some are differentiated fetters: restlessness in one who relishes the superior dhyāna, conceit in one with conceit in the superior dhyāna, and ignorance in one with ignorance in the superior dhyāna.

items.title: Five Causes of Faithless Rigidity That Stunt Every Wholesome Root, and Five Obstacles to Genuine Diligence

items.zh: 又為五種不信敬所執持者，心不調柔，不能生長諸善根本。謂於大師所說正法，增上戒學、增上心學、增上慧學、正覺發者、正教授者、正教誡者同梵行所，無有信敬。又有五種為斷煩惱正精進障。一者、耽著等至及生；二者、耽著利養恭敬；三者、放逸；四者、惡慧；五者、其心下劣，或增上慢。
items.en: One held by five kinds of faithlessness and disrespect has a mind that remains rigid and cannot grow any wholesome root: namely, having no trust or respect for the true teaching spoken by the Great Teacher, for the higher training in precepts, in concentration, and in wisdom, or for those fellow practitioners who rightly awaken, rightly instruct, and rightly admonish. There are also five obstacles to the correct diligence that severs affliction: first, being absorbed in meditative attainment and [craving] rebirth thereby; second, being absorbed in gain and veneration; third, carelessness; fourth, faulty discernment; fifth, a mind that is either unworthily timid or inflated with false confidence.

items.title: Five Wrong Ways to Treat an Enemy and Their Exact Consequences, and Five Losses That Bring Grief in This Life and the Next

items.zh: 復有不能堪忍補特伽羅，於他怨敵所起五種邪行。謂不堪忍者，於他怨敵先起瞋心怨嫌意樂；於彼親友樂欲破壞；常欲令彼發生憂苦，廣作一切不饒益事；壞自所受清淨尸羅；由身語意多行惡行。由此五種惡邪行故，能感後世還來此中三種等流過患，一種現法等流過患，一種後法異熟過患。謂此生中，多諸怨敵；親友乖離；由他發起種種憂苦、不可愛事恒現在前；臨命終時多生憂悔；命終已後顛墜惡趣。與此相違，能堪忍者，於他怨敵發起五種正行。由此所感勝利差別，如應當知。又有五法，能生現法後法一切憂苦。一、親屬滅亡，二、所有財寶非理喪失，三、疾病緣身。此三能生現法憂苦。四、毀犯尸羅，五、毀謗一切諸惡邪見。此二能生後法憂苦。
items.en: There is also the intolerant person, who gives rise to five wrong reactions towards an enemy: giving rise to hostile, resentful intent towards the enemy first of all; wishing to destroy the enemy's friendships; constantly wishing the enemy to suffer grief, doing everything possible to harm them; ruining one's own pure precepts thereby; and, through body, speech, and mind, committing much unwholesome conduct. [The consequences:] in a life when one returns here, many enemies; estrangement from one's own friends; others constantly bringing about grief and disagreeable circumstances; at the time of death, much regret; and after death, falling into an evil destiny. The reverse of this — the tolerant person — gives rise to five right reactions towards an enemy. There are also five things that produce all grief, in this life and the next: first, the loss of family; second, the unreasonable loss of wealth; third, illness afflicting the body — these three produce grief in this very life. Fourth, violating one's precepts; fifth, slandering [the three jewels] through evil, wrong views — these two produce grief in the next life.

items.zh: 與此相違五法，當知能生現法後法所有喜樂。

items.title: What an Arhat Transcends Even in Ordinary Daily Necessities, and the Five Factors That Bring Swift Realisation

items.zh: 又阿羅漢，雖現追求供身財物，亦常受用，而能超度三邪追求、二邪受用。謂能超過殺生、偷盜、妄語所引三邪追求，亦能超過妻妾、畜積二邪受用。又修斷者成就五法，隨其所欲，於諸善品方便修行，亦能速證究竟通慧。一者、於所修斷猛利樂欲，如教奉行；二者、於自所有如實發露；三者、身力康強；四者、相續無間修方便中，其心勇銳；五者、成就通達止、舉、捨相時分智慧。
items.en: An arhat, though still outwardly seeking and regularly using the material things that support the body, has nonetheless transcended three wrong forms of seeking and two wrong forms of enjoyment: transcending the three wrong forms of seeking driven by killing, stealing, and lying, and transcending the two wrong forms of enjoyment — a spouse, and hoarded stores. One who cultivates severance and accomplishes five things is thereby able, at will, to skilfully cultivate every wholesome quality and swiftly realise ultimate penetrating wisdom: first, fierce aspiration towards what is to be cultivated, practised exactly as taught; second, honest disclosure of one's own faults; third, robust bodily strength; fourth, unbroken, courageous diligence in sustained practice; fifth, thorough mastery of the timing of calming, uplifting, and equanimity.

blocks.text: Today's fives include a passage of practical ethics many readers find striking: five wrong ways to treat an enemy, with their consequences, and a Yogācāra reading of what an "enemy" is.

Stinginess about one's dwelling, one's family of supporters, gifts, praise, and the Dharma. The *Pīxún jì* takes the list from the *Satyasiddhi*. Stinginess with the Dharma is the subtlest, and, as Venerable Miào Jìng said of Cūḍapanthaka (Day 54), leads to dullness.

subs.head: Five hindrances, five lower and five higher fetters

blocks.text: The five hindrances ruin precepts, learning, and meditation in sequence (Day 77). The **five lower fetters**: self-view, doubt, grasping at precepts, sensual desire, ill will. The **five higher fetters**: craving for form existence, craving for formless existence, restlessness, conceit, and ignorance. Master Cháng Bǎi: the higher fetters describe three different practitioners: one who relishes the absorptions and grows restless, one who grows conceited by comparison, and one who remains deluded.

Five causes of faithless rigidity stunt every wholesome root: lack of faith in the teacher, the Dharma, the trainings, and fellow practitioners. Master Cháng Bǎi: the fellow practitioners who "rightly awaken" and "rightly instruct" are one's preceptor and one's teacher of meditation and wisdom.

subs.head: Five wrong ways to treat an enemy

blocks.text: Responding to an enemy with wrong reactions brings consequences that, the *Pīxún jì* says, "return here in a later life": ugliness, unhappiness, loss of wealth, and so on; and regret at death in this life. The tolerant person reacts rightly.

Master Cháng Bǎi gives the Yogācāra reading: "The enemy is not outside; the main cause is the false discrimination in one's own mind, summoned by past or present wrongdoing." This is consciousness-only applied to conflict. The other person is real, but what makes him an "enemy" is the mind's construction and the karma that brought the encounter. Working on that construction is within one's power.

subs.head: An arhat in daily life; five factors for swift realisation

blocks.text: An arhat transcends five things even in eating, dressing, and lodging. Five factors bring swift realisation; the second is "honest disclosure of one's own faults". Master Cháng Bǎi: "If each time one discloses and then keeps doing it, one has no sincere intention to change." Confession is only honest when it includes the resolve to stop.

quiz.q: Which treatise does the Pixunji cite for the five kinds of stinginess here?
options: the Satyasiddhi, chapter on mixed afflictions: stinginess about dwelling, family, giving, praise, and Dharma
quiz.why: The *Pixunji*: "The *Satyasiddhi*, chapter on mixed afflictions, lists five kinds of stinginess: about dwelling, family, giving, praise, and Dharma; these five correspond in order." Venerable Miào Jìng stresses it is Kumārajīva's *Satyasiddhi*, not the *Cheng weishi lun*.

quiz.q: The English renders all three differentiated fetters with "one who craves them." How do the lectures read them?
options: three different people: one who relishes the absorptions and grows restless, one who becomes conceited about them, one ignorant regarding them
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the practitioner relishes the absorption attained and the mind grows restless; or, from competitive conceit, cultivates concentration and grows conceited once it is attained. The original names three distinct people; the English collapses them into "craves."

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi identify the fellow practitioners who "rightly awaken, rightly instruct, and rightly admonish"?
options: the awakener is one's preceptor; the instructor is the teacher of concentration and wisdom, the instructing ācārya
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the one who rightly awakens is the fellow practitioner who awakens one's wisdom — one's preceptor; the one who rightly instructs is the spiritual friend teaching concentration and wisdom — the instructing ācārya. Venerable Miào Jìng agrees.

quiz.q: The English places the first three consequences "in this very life." When does the Pixunji say they occur?
options: the first three are outflows "returning here in a later life"; the fourth, regret at death, is a present-life outflow; the fifth, falling, a later-life ripening; f14 omits the "later life" line
quiz.why: The *Pixunji*: the first three wrong reactions bring three outflow consequences "returning here in a later life"; "in this life, many enemies" refers to that later life. Venerable Miào Jìng: having estranged an enemy's friends before, one is now estranged from one's own.

quiz.q: The tolerant person reacts rightly to enemies. From the Yogācāra view, where does Master Cháng Bǎi locate the main cause of an enemy?
options: the enemy is not outside — the main cause is one's own false discrimination, summoned by past or present wrong deeds
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The enemy is not outside; the main cause is the false discrimination in one's own mind, one's own wrong deeds of past or present lives summoning the enemy's appearance." Venerable Miào Jìng: even if wronged, keep the mind pure.

quiz.q: The second factor is "honest disclosure of one's own faults." What makes it honest, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: sincerely reforming — confessing then repeating the same act each time shows no sincere wish to change
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "If each time one discloses and then keeps doing it, one has no sincere intention to change — confessing the same thing every time is not earnestly, sincerely reforming." Robust strength, per the *Pixunji*, comes from eating in moderation.
